content: Hepatitis B vaccination is the most effective method to prevent infection with the hepatitis B virus (HBV) and its associated complications, including liver cirrhosis, liver cancer, liver failure, and death. The vaccine is particularly important for individuals at higher risk of HBV infection, such as heterosexuals with multiple sexual partners, injection drug users, men who have sex with men (MSM), and household contacts or sexual partners of individuals with chronic HBV infection. The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) has issued updated recommendations to increase hepatitis B vaccination coverage among adults at risk for HBV infection. These updates are part of a comprehensive strategy to eliminate HBV transmission in the United States. The first part of the ACIP statement, which focused on vaccination of infants, children, and adolescents, was previously published. The second part of the statement addresses adult vaccination and provides guidance on implementation strategies to ensure that at-risk adults are vaccinated. HBV is a DNA virus that primarily replicates in the liver. After exposure, the virus enters the liver via the bloodstream. HBV infection can be asymptomatic or symptomatic, with an average incubation period of 90 days. Symptoms, when present, may include anorexia, malaise, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and jaundice. Chronic HBV infection can lead to cirrhosis, liver cancer, and liver failure. Approximately 95% of primary HBV infections in immunocompetent adults resolve spontaneously, resulting in lasting immunity. However, chronic infection occurs in 90% of infected infants, 30% of children under 5 years old, and 5% of adults. Hepatitis B vaccination has been successfully integrated into the childhood immunization schedule, with high coverage rates among infants and adolescents. Universal vaccination of infants beginning at birth, routine screening of pregnant women for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), and post-exposure prophylaxis for infants born to HBsAg-positive mothers have significantly reduced perinatal HBV transmission. Vaccination coverage among adolescents has also increased substantially, with approximately 50-60% of adolescents aged 13-15 years completing the three-dose vaccine series by 2003. Between 1990 and 2005, the incidence of acute hepatitis B in the United States declined by 78%, with a 96% reduction among children and adolescents. Despite these successes, the incidence of acute hepatitis B remains highest among adults, who accounted for 95% of an estimated 51,000 new HBV infections in 2005. Adults at risk for HBV infection include those with sexual exposure (e.g., individuals with multiple sexual partners, MSM), injection drug users, household contacts of individuals with chronic HBV infection, healthcare workers, and travelers to HBV-endemic regions. The ACIP recommends universal hepatitis B vaccination for all adults who have not completed the vaccine series, with a focus on those at increased risk. HBV is transmitted through percutaneous or mucosal exposure to infectious blood or body fluids, including serum, semen, and saliva. The virus is highly stable in the environment and can remain viable on surfaces for more than seven days. Sexual contact and percutaneous exposure (e.g., injection drug use, needlestick injuries) are the primary modes of HBV transmission among adults. Routine blood donor screening and viral inactivation procedures have made transfusion-related HBV transmission rare in the United States. Chronic HBV infection serves as the main reservoir for ongoing transmission. Individuals with chronic infection may remain asymptomatic until the onset of cirrhosis or end-stage liver disease. Periodic screening with ultrasonography and alpha-fetoprotein testing can aid in the early detection of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), improving survival outcomes. Antiviral therapies approved by the FDA can achieve sustained suppression of HBV replication and remission of liver disease in some patients with chronic infection. Serologic markers are used to diagnose and monitor HBV infection. The presence of HBsAg indicates active infection, while anti-HBs indicates immunity. Anti-HBc persists for life after infection and can help distinguish between acute, resolving, and chronic infection. HBV DNA testing can detect viral replication and guide management decisions. In summary, hepatitis B vaccination is a critical public health measure to prevent HBV infection and its complications. Efforts to increase vaccination coverage among at-risk adults, combined with ongoing surveillance and education, are essential to achieving the goal of HBV elimination in the United States.
